messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: implicit functions and stan
parts:
One area where stan could have a clear advantage wrt BUGS is if it
could support implicit functions. See

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicit_and_explicit_functions

for details.

Basically, suppose we want to specify that rho is such that

g(rho | theta, x) = 0

but it is not practical or possible to write rho as an explicit
function of theta (and x) like we typically would:

parameters {
double theta;
}

derived parameters {
double rho;
rho <- 42 * theta;
}

To deal with this, somebody would need a C++ function that solved the
implicit function for rho with something like

while(fabs(g(rho | theta, x)) > TOLERANCE) {
// update rho
}

Stan already handles this sort of thing by just rolling the chain rule
through the process of numerically solving for the parameter (as in
eigenvalues and whatnot). But, keeping track of the derivatives could
be very slow and memory intensive considering that after you
eventually find a rho that implies

g(rho | theta, x) = 0

then it is simple to obtain the derivative of a another function of
rho and theta (e.g. a log density) wrt to theta that properly accounts
for the fact that rho is really a function of theta:

(d rho) / (d theta) = - [ (d g(rho | theta, x) / (d theta) ] / [ (d
g(rho | theta, x) / (d rho) ]

So, how can we teach stan implicit differentiation and is the 1.x API
equipped to add such a feature in the forseeable future? Would we need
an

implicitly defined parameters {
double rho;
// Hello Stan, there will have been a functor somewhere defining
g(rho | theta, x);
// Plz solve for rho and leaf the implicit derivative onto theta's
tree;
}

or similar?

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implicit functions and stan
parts:
I don't quite understand the details.

At the risk of being obvious, anything for
which we can somehow implement a function and
somehow implement a derivative is fair game.

If there's error approximating the derivative,
it'll affect the accuracy of the Hamiltonian
simulation. I think that just means a higher
rejection rate if it's less accurate, not a broken
algorithm.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: implicit functions and stan
parts:
It's obvious for explicit functions that stan can handle the
derivatives with AD.

It's not obvious but true and really cool that stan can produce a
derivative with AD in situations where we can only numerically
approximate the function. So, I am pretty sure we could upgrade the
parser to handle something like

double(0,1) rho;
rho <- 0.5;
rho <- numerically_solve(rho, g(rho | theta, x), TOLERANCE);
}

But numerically_solve() is going to propagate a ton of AD calculations
that aren't conceptually necessary because we can calculate the
derivative of rho wrt theta from the ratio of the derivatives of g(rho
| theta, x) wrt rho and theta. So, it is almost like we need to tell
stan to skip the AD calculations inside numerically_solve() and
afterward graft the implicit derivative onto the tree in the right
place. That sounds theoretically possible, but I don't know if we have
the flexibility to do that yet.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: implicit functions and stan
parts:
We can code anything for which we can code
g(x) and its derivative g'(x). It doesn't matter
if g(x) is solved numerically by iteration and
g'(x) is computed analytically. In fact, we'll
run into this case with cumulative densities.

But that can't be what you're asking.

The issue must be can we somehow define a function
g(...) in Stan and then automatically solve it
and automatically differentiate it. I don't see
why not, though there's nothing like that in there
now. Matt's been talking about adding solvers
that could themselves be based on auto-dif.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: implicit functions and stan
parts:
Right. Prerequisites for this feature would be

-- a C++ function to numerically solve an equation in one variable
-- a way for the parser to get the equation to be solved from
the .stan file to the numerical solver.

But, it would be even better if we could short-circuit the AD.

Say we have an explicit log-density function

f(y | theta, rho)

but with a constraint on the parameters

rho^5 - rho == theta

from which we get g(rho | theta) = rho^5 - rho - theta .

It is impossible for the user to write rho as an explicit function of
theta:

rho <- ???
}

but the user could write something like this

rho <- 1.0;
rho <- numerically_solve(rho, rho^5 - rho - theta);
}

The way stan is now, there would be a lot of AD going on inside
numerically_solve(). But humans know that for any rho that satisfies
the constraint,

[d rho] / [d theta] = 1 / (5 * rho^4 - 1)

via the implicit function theorem. In other words, I think the brute
force approach of propagating AD through a while loop would create a
big branch on the tree that ultimately accounts for [d rho] / [d
theta] when we already know its formula but can't evaluate it until we
get rho.

So, can we program stan to not create a big branch of AD to calculate
[d rho] / [d theta] while numerically_solve() is finding rho, but
instead wait until rho is found, and then put the value of 1 / (5 *
rho^4 - 1) wherever it needs to go?

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: implicit functions and stan
parts:
Yes, you don't need to auto-dif an iterative function.

One advice in the literature is to only auto-dif
the last few stages of it.

The concrete example helped immensely. Is there an
actual application for which you'd like to do this?

The way I see it going, we'd:

a) let the user define an equation as in your
example, which implicitly defines a function f()

b) auto-dif the bits of the definition of f()
in an iterative solver, and then

c) use the implicit function theorem to propagate
derivatives of the function.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: implicit functions and stan
parts:
One perhaps motivating example is the so-called "generalized lambda
distribution".

http://www.stat.ucl.ac.be/ISdidactique/Rhelp/library/Davies/html/Gld.html

The GLD cannot express its PDF or its CDF in closed form. Rather, the
distribution is defined by the inverse of the CDF, say Q(p | lambda).

To indirectly evaluate the density, f(y | lambda), you first have to
numerically find the value of the CDF, p = F(y | lambda), such that
Q(p | lambda) == y.

Given p, the value of the density is known to be something like 1 /
Q'(p | lambda).

So, that is an example where in order for the user to model something
(basically anything continuous and unimodal) with a GLD, stan would
have to internally do some efficient numeric solving, implicit
differentiation, etc.

Since that is internal, maybe that is an easier starting point than
the more general case where the user (often economists) have some
arbitrary constraint they need to impose on the parameters, like the
rho^5 - rho == theta example, where we would have to parse an
arbitrary implicit function in order to pass to the numeric solver.

Ben
